notes.h: The roots of anti-Semitism and Nazi racial ideology
notes.b: Hatred of Jews was centuries old in Europe before the Nazis. What Hitler's movement added was a racial doctrine that made Jews the enemy of the German nation, and then turned that doctrine into state policy.
points: Anti-Semitism, hostility towards or prejudice against Jews, combined religious hostility from Christian teaching, economic resentment and, from the late nineteenth century, racial theories that claimed Jews were a separate and inferior race. There is more on this in the notes on Europe before 1914.
Three examples show how widespread it was before the Nazis: pogroms (violent attacks on Jewish communities) in the Russian Empire from 1881 and the Dreyfus Affair in France, which began in 1894.
The third example is the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a forgery first published in Russia in 1903, which invented a Jewish plot to rule the world and so gave hatred a false 'proof'.

The Nazis shifted anti-Semitism from religion to race. Under the old religious hatred a Jew could escape by converting, but under racial anti-Semitism ancestry was all that counted, so conversion or assimilation could never make a Jew 'German'.
notes.tip: Examiners want 'Europe', not only Germany, so mention Italy's 1938 racial laws as well as Nazi Germany. Define anti-Semitism in a sentence, since it is a key concept.

notes.h: Nazi racial ideology, Mein Kampf and herrenvolk
notes.b: The Nazis built their politics on the idea that races struggle for survival. This gave Jews a fixed role as the enemy, and it gave the regime a reason for its later policies.
points: Nazi racial ideology saw history as a struggle between races, with the so-called 'Aryans' at the top. Jews were portrayed as a racial enemy working behind both capitalism and communism.
Hitler's Mein Kampf (first volume 1925) blamed Jews for Germany's defeat in 1918, for communism and for the Versailles settlement, and it set out the aim of removing Jews from German life.

This blame built on the 'stab in the back' myth, the false claim that Germany lost the war because of betrayal at home, and on resentment of the hyperinflation of the early 1920s, so many Germans were ready to listen.

Herrenvolk, the 'master race' of Germanic people, was the key Nazi concept. It required that Jews be defined as racially alien and excluded from the German community, while Slavs were labelled Untermenschen ('subhumans'). Lebensraum (living space) in the east later brought millions more Jews under German rule.

The Nazis came to power when Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Their tools were the SS under Heinrich Himmler (Reichsführer-SS), the Gestapo (secret police) and concentration camps, the first of which, Dachau, opened in March 1933.
Anti-Semitism was not confined to Germany: in 1938 Italy introduced racial laws that excluded Jews from schools, the professions and the armed forces and banned mixed marriages.
notes.tip: Examiners want 'Europe', not only Germany, so mention Italy's 1938 racial laws as well as Nazi Germany. Define herrenvolk in a sentence, since it is a key concept.

notes.h: Propaganda and the Jews of Germany in 1933
notes.b: Nazi ideas reached ordinary Germans through newspapers, films and classrooms. The target of this hatred was a small minority that was mostly well integrated.
points: Der Stürmer, the anti-Semitic weekly of Julius Streicher (founded 1923), promoted stereotypes of Jews and encouraged hostility towards Jewish neighbours.

Schools taught race 'science', so children learned that Germans and Jews belonged to different races. Two films, The Eternal Jew (Der ewige Jude) and Jud Süß, both of 1940, presented Jews as a threat.
There were about 500,000 Jews in Germany in 1933, under one per cent of the population, which shows how little real basis the 'Jewish threat' had.
Most German Jews were fully integrated into German economic, cultural and civic life, which is why the racial claims had to be imposed by law, and many had served in the First World War.

notes.b: Once in power, the regime set out to push Jews out of public life, first by pressure and then by law. The Nuremberg Laws gave this exclusion a legal basis.
points: The boycott of Jewish shops and businesses on 1 April 1933 was announced as a one-day action and lasted one day. Public response was mixed, so the regime moved on to using the law instead.

The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (7 April 1933) dismissed Jewish officials. Later measures excluded Jews from the law, medicine, journalism, culture and the universities, and in May 1933 Nazi book burnings destroyed works by Jewish authors.
The Nuremberg Laws of 15 September 1935, announced at the Nuremberg rally of that year, were the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour.
The Reich Citizenship Law removed German citizenship from Jews, who became subjects with no political rights, and the second law banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and Germans.

The laws did not say who counted as a Jew. A supplementary decree of 14 November 1935 defined a Jew by descent, with three or four Jewish grandparents, and people of mixed descent were classed as Mischlinge. This definition was used in later persecution.
notes.tip: Date the Nuremberg Laws exactly (15 September 1935) and do not confuse them with the Nuremberg rallies or the Nuremberg trials of 1945-46. The definition of a Jew by grandparents came in the November decree, not the September laws.

notes.b: As the economic and social exclusion tightened, Jews lost their livelihoods and many tried to leave. Leaving was hard, and this is why so many could not.
points: 'Aryanisation' meant forcing Jews to sell their businesses and property at low prices, or confiscating them, so that wealth passed to non-Jewish Germans. Jews had to register their property in 1938, which made seizure easier, and the process accelerated that year.
After the Anschluss (union of Austria with Germany) in March 1938, the Jews of Vienna suffered public humiliation and violence.
About 280,000 Jews had left Germany by September 1939, and about 117,000 more left annexed Austria.
Emigration was difficult because emigrants lost their property and faced emigration taxes, and then needed visas and had to meet immigration limits in the countries abroad.

notes.b: Kristallnacht marked the move from legal discrimination to open, state-encouraged violence. It was triggered by a chain of events in autumn 1938.
points: In late October 1938 Polish Jews living in Germany were expelled to the Polish border. Herschel Grynszpan, 17, whose family had been expelled, shot the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris on 7 November 1938.
Vom Rath died on 9 November. That evening Goebbels gave a speech to party leaders in Munich that launched a pogrom, an organised attack on Jews.

Kristallnacht ('Night of Broken Glass'), 9-10 November 1938, took place in Germany and Austria, so it was a violent event on a national scale. Over 250 synagogues were burned or destroyed, about 7,500 Jewish businesses and many Jewish homes were wrecked and about 90 Jews were killed.
About 30,000 Jewish men were sent to Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen, and most were released only if they agreed to emigrate.
Jews were made to pay a collective fine of one billion Reichsmarks, so the victims paid for the damage done to them, and were then excluded from economic life and from German schools.
notes.tip: Do not say the shooting and the pogrom happened on the same day: vom Rath was shot on 7 November and died on 9 November. A cause and result chain scores well: vom Rath's death, Kristallnacht, mass arrests, the fine and exclusion from the economy.

notes.h: The refugee crisis: Évian and the Kindertransport
notes.b: Violence in Germany and Austria sent thousands of Jews looking for a place to go. Other states mostly refused to take them in, which made emigration a trap for many.
points: The Évian Conference (July 1938, at Évian-les-Bains, France) was called on the initiative of President Franklin Roosevelt of the United States. 32 countries attended, but almost none agreed to take more refugees, so the conference achieved little.
Only the Dominican Republic offered to take a substantial number of refugees.
Immigration limits and visa rules kept most refugees out, so even Jews with the means to leave often could not find a country willing to admit them.

The Kindertransport (December 1938 to September 1939) took about 10,000 children, mostly Jewish, from Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia to Britain. Their parents were not admitted, so most children left without them.
notes.tip: Distinguish Évian (1938, refugees) from Wannsee (1942, deportation and murder). Also distinguish the Kindertransport (children to Britain, 1938-39) from the Danish rescue (to Sweden, 1943).

notes.b: The war put millions more Jews under German rule. The regime responded by confining them in ghettos, where conditions killed many even before any deportation.
points: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and about 3 million Jews in Poland came under German or Soviet rule. From December 1939 Jews in the General Government (the German-ruled part of occupied Poland) had to wear armbands marked with a Star of David.
Property was seized throughout the occupied territories.
The Madagascar Plan (1940) proposed deporting Jews overseas to the island of Madagascar. It was abandoned when Britain was not defeated.

Ghettos, sealed-off districts of cities, were set up in Polish cities. The Łódź ghetto was sealed in 1940, and the Warsaw ghetto, sealed in November 1940, was the largest, with about 400,000 people at its height.
Jewish Councils (Judenräte, singular Judenrat) were forced to administer the ghettos. Whether their members acted wrongly is debated, but they were coerced and are not counted as collaborators.
Ghetto conditions were marked by overcrowding, starvation rations, typhus (a disease spread by lice) and forced labour, so death rates were high before any deportation began.
notes.tip: The invasion of Poland and Barbarossa put millions more Jews under German rule, which led to ghettos, mass shootings and then industrial killing. Use that chain in an essay.

notes.b: When Germany invaded the Soviet Union, killing in the east became organised and open. Jews were shot in large numbers close to their homes.
points: The Einsatzgruppen were four mobile killing units, A to D, of the SS and police. They followed the army into the Soviet Union after the invasion (Operation Barbarossa) of 22 June 1941.
They shot Jews, Roma and communist officials, helped by German police battalions and local auxiliaries, which meant that killing could be done fast and in the open.
At Babi Yar, a ravine near Kiev, about 33,000 Jews were shot on 29-30 September 1941. It was a mass shooting, not a camp, so do not describe it as a death camp.
In Germany the yellow star became compulsory for Jews from September 1941, and deportations of German Jews to the east began in October 1941.
notes.tip: Einsatzgruppen were mobile killing squads, not the Sonderkommando (Jewish prisoners forced to work in the crematoria) and not the Judenrat. Know the date, June 1941, and name Babi Yar.

notes.h: The decision for genocide and the Wannsee Conference
notes.b: Mass murder grew in 1941 as the war widened. The Wannsee Conference then coordinated the machinery across the government, rather than starting the killing.
points: Historians agree that the murder of the Jews grew during 1941, but no written Hitler order survives. Göring gave Reinhard Heydrich a written order on 31 July 1941 to prepare a 'total solution' of the Jewish question.
Himmler, head of the SS, was overall in charge, while Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office, was the organiser. Heydrich was assassinated in Prague in 1942.
The Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942, held at a villa at Wannsee, Berlin, was chaired by Heydrich. About 15 senior officials attended, and Adolf Eichmann kept the minutes.

The conference coordinated the deportation of all European Jews. It brought the ministries into line with a policy already under way. The phrase 'Final Solution' was in use before the conference, and means the Nazi plan to murder all the Jews of Europe.
The minutes listed about 11 million Jews to be included, even in neutral and unoccupied countries. Britain was included, and Ireland was listed with 4,000.

Historians debate whether the Holocaust was planned from the start or developed step by step: intentionalists stress Hitler's early plan, and functionalists stress the growth of policy under pressure of events.
notes.tip: Say who chaired Wannsee (Heydrich) and who kept the minutes (Eichmann). Himmler, Heydrich, Eichmann and Göring are easy to confuse: Göring signed the July 1941 order. For a 6-mark question on the Final Solution, say it was the Nazi plan to murder all the Jews of Europe.

notes.b: The killing now moved to camps built for the purpose. Knowing the difference between types of camp, and naming the main death camps, is basic to any answer.
points: A concentration camp was a prison and labour camp, such as Dachau, Buchenwald and Bergen-Belsen, where many died of disease and starvation. A death (extermination) camp was built for killing. Bergen-Belsen and Dachau were not death camps, because they were built for imprisonment, not for killing.

All six death camps were in occupied Poland. Chełmno used gas vans from December 1941, and the Operation Reinhard camps of Bełżec, Sobibór and Treblinka opened in 1942. Majdanek, near Lublin, and Auschwitz-Birkenau were both labour and death camps, which is why they are listed in both groups.
Treblinka was a pure killing centre, built only for murder, and estimates of its dead range from about 700,000 to about 900,000. The Reinhard camps killed most arrivals within hours.

Auschwitz, near Oświęcim, had three parts: the main camp (Auschwitz I), Birkenau (Auschwitz II), where the gas chambers were, and Monowitz (Auschwitz III), where prisoners did labour for IG Farben, a chemical company.
At Auschwitz Zyklon B poison gas was used. About 1.1 million people were murdered there, about 1 million of them Jews. On the arrival ramp prisoners were selected for labour or for immediate death.
Staff and gassing techniques from the T4 programme against disabled people were later used in the death camps, so the programme was a rehearsal for mass murder.
notes.tip: Name at least two death camps, and do not call Dachau or Bergen-Belsen death camps. Examiners reward the concentration camp and death camp distinction.

notes.h: Deportations, death marches and the scale of the murders
notes.b: Jews were brought to the camps from across Europe by rail. The numbers lost varied sharply from country to country, which depended on who ruled and who helped.
points: Eichmann's office organised the deportation transports by rail from across Europe, including the round-ups of Jews in France.
Germany occupied Hungary in March 1944, and about 430,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz in about eight weeks between May and July 1944. Most were murdered on arrival.
As Soviet forces advanced in late 1944 and 1945, the SS forced prisoners west into Germany on death marches. Very many died of exhaustion, cold and shooting.
About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust (the Hebrew word is Shoah, 'catastrophe'), about 3 million of them from Poland.
Losses by country varied: about 90 per cent of Polish Jews and of the Jews of the Baltic states, about 75 per cent of Dutch Jews and about 25 per cent of French Jews.
Anne Frank, who hid in Amsterdam, was deported in 1944 and died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945. Her diary, published after the war, is one individual record of the victims.
notes.tip: Give the six million as 'about'. For Hungary, say about 430,000 in about eight weeks between May and July 1944.

notes.h: Other victims of Nazi racial policy
notes.b: The regime's racial ideology did not stop with Jews. It also led to the persecution and murder of other groups seen as inferior or as threats to the 'national community'.
points: A sterilisation law of July 1933 allowed compulsory sterilisation of people with hereditary conditions, and about 400,000 people were sterilised.

The Aktion T4 programme, begun in 1939, murdered about 70,000 disabled patients in gas chambers by August 1941. It was officially halted that month after public protests, including a sermon by Bishop Galen, though killing of patients continued in secret.
Roma and Sinti, treated as racially inferior because of the same race ideas, were deported, imprisoned and murdered. Estimates of the dead range from about 200,000 to 500,000.
About 3 million of some 5.7 million Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity, from starvation, disease and execution.
Homosexual men were arrested under Paragraph 175 of the criminal code, Jehovah's Witnesses were persecuted for refusing military service and loyalty oaths, and political opponents were imprisoned.
Slavs in Poland were treated as a labour reserve, and their intelligentsia, the educated leaders of society, was targeted.

notes.b: Resistance was real but limited, because the Germans controlled weapons and information and the ghettos were sealed. It took armed and unarmed forms.
points: The Warsaw ghetto uprising ran from 19 April to 16 May 1943. The Jewish Fighting Organisation (ŻOB), led by Mordechai Anielewicz, resisted the attempt to deport the remaining inhabitants, after mass deportations to Treblinka in summer 1942. The ghetto was destroyed, and Anielewicz was killed in May 1943.
Prisoners revolted in the camps: at Treblinka in August 1943, at Sobibór in October 1943, where they killed guards and escaped, and in the Sonderkommando revolt at Auschwitz-Birkenau in October 1944.
Jewish partisans fought in the forests of Eastern Europe. The Bielski brothers' group in Belorussia sheltered about 1,200 Jews.
Unarmed resistance included smuggling food and arms into the ghettos, keeping diaries and maintaining schools, religious and cultural life.
Emanuel Ringelblum's secret archive (Oneg Shabbat) in the Warsaw ghetto recorded life there. It was buried in milk cans and metal boxes and was partly recovered after the war.
notes.tip: Do not mix the Warsaw ghetto uprising (Jewish fighters, April-May 1943) with the Warsaw Uprising of the Polish Home Army in 1944. They are different events.

notes.h: Collaborators, bystanders, rescuers and the Allies
notes.b: Whether Jews lived or died depended greatly on how other Europeans behaved. Some helped the killers, many stood by, some risked their lives, and the Allies debated how far they could act.
points: Collaborators were governments, police and officials who helped persecute Jews. Vichy France issued its first anti-Jewish statute in October 1940, French police took part in round-ups, Dutch officials helped, and in Lithuania most Jews were murdered in 1941 with local auxiliaries taking part.
Bystanders did nothing, out of indifference or fear. Some neighbours profited from the seizure of Jewish property, and the churches' public protest was limited.
Rescuers hid Jews, forged documents and smuggled people across borders. Yad Vashem in Jerusalem (founded 1953) honours non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews as the Righteous Among the Nations.

Oskar Schindler, a German industrialist in Kraków, saved about 1,200 Jews by employing them in his factories. Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat in Budapest in 1944, issued protective passports to Jews.
In Denmark in October 1943 over 7,000 Jews were ferried to safety in Sweden. This showed that large-scale protection was possible where the population and the local authorities were willing to act.
The Allies knew of the mass murder by 1942, and on 17 December 1942 issued a declaration condemning the extermination of the Jews.

The Allies did not bomb Auschwitz or the railways leading to it, and immigration limits stayed in place, so rescue was left mostly to individuals. Whether more could have been done is debated, for example whether bombing would have saved lives.
notes.tip: Bring in countries other than Germany: Vichy France, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Hungary, Denmark and the Allies. Do not call the Judenräte collaborators.

notes.b: Liberation revealed the scale of the crimes to the world, and trials set legal standards. The effects continued after 1945.
points: Soviet troops liberated Majdanek in July 1944 and Auschwitz on 27 January 1945. American troops liberated Buchenwald and Dachau, and the British liberated Bergen-Belsen on 15 April 1945.
Newsreels and photographs of the camps shocked the world, because they gave proof that could not be denied.
The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg sat from November 1945 to October 1946 and tried 22 leading Nazis. Its charges included the new charge of crimes against humanity.
Later trials prosecuted doctors, judges, industrialists, SS and camp staff. Eichmann was captured in Argentina in 1960, tried in Jerusalem in 1961 and executed in 1962.

Raphael Lemkin coined the word 'genocide' in 1944, and the UN Genocide Convention was adopted in December 1948. Many Jewish displaced persons, survivors with no home to return to, left Europe for Palestine, and the State of Israel was founded in May 1948.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Nuremberg trials (1945-46) with the Nuremberg Laws (1935). Liberation dates to know: Auschwitz on 27 January 1945.

notes.h: Assessment: how anti-Semitism and the Holocaust affected Europe
notes.b: The effects reached every part of Europe, and historians weigh them as pairs: destruction against rescue, complicity against resistance, and contemporary views against later ones.
points: Destruction: Jewish communities and their culture were destroyed across Europe, so Europe lost much of its Jewish population. Rescue: the Righteous Among the Nations and the Danish rescue saved many.

Complicity: states, collaborators and bystanders helped or allowed the killing, for example Vichy France and Lithuanian auxiliaries. Resistance: ghetto fighters, camp revolts and partisans fought back, and Ringelblum's archive preserved the record.

Refugee crisis: Évian and immigration limits showed that most states would not solve the crisis. Legacy: Nuremberg, the idea of crimes against humanity and the Genocide Convention made genocide a crime in law.

Contemporary view: in the 1930s and 1940s many contemporaries treated persecution as Germany's internal affair or did not believe the reports. Later view: Allied governments knew of the mass killings by 1942, and historians debate whether more could have been done.
Historians debate intentionalist and functionalist explanations: was the murder planned from the start, or did it develop step by step as the war went on?

They also debate why ordinary men became killers. Christopher Browning's Ordinary Men (1992) described a German police battalion's killings, while Daniel Goldhagen's Hitler's Willing Executioners (1996) argued for a deep German 'eliminationist' anti-Semitism, a view widely criticised by historians.
notes.tip: For the Higher Level essay (100 marks), argue a thesis and organise by effect: ideology, persecution in Germany and Austria, the refugee crisis, genocide, complicity versus resistance, and legacy. A short balanced paragraph on one debate earns overall-evaluation marks.

keyTerms.definition: Hostility towards and discrimination against Jews, which the Nazi regime turned into a racial doctrine and state policy.
The systematic murder of about six million European Jews by the Nazi regime and its collaborators between 1941 and 1945.
The Nazi idea of a master race of Germanic people, used to justify racial hierarchy and the persecution of Jews and others.
The laws of 15 September 1935 that defined Jews by descent, removed their citizenship and banned marriage with people of German blood.
The pogrom of 9 and 10 November 1938, when Nazi supporters destroyed synagogues and Jewish property across Germany and Austria.
Mobile SS and police units that followed the German army into the Soviet Union and carried out mass shootings of Jews and others from June 1941.
The meeting of 20 January 1942 near Berlin that coordinated the deportation and murder of European Jews under the Final Solution.
A section of a city in which Jews were confined under Nazi rule, often sealed off from the outside world and used for forced labour.
The Nazi term for the plan to murder all the Jews of Europe, set out at Wannsee in January 1942.
The forced transfer of Jewish businesses and property to non-Jewish owners at low prices.
A Jewish Council set up by the Germans in a ghetto to carry out their orders.
The title given by Yad Vashem in Jerusalem to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews.
